title: Make a Decision
content:
What problem does this solve?
Before this lesson, Python follows instructions in order. After it, your program can choose what happens based on its data — investigate a strange camp, or mark it clear.

Basic syntax
  if bedrolls < registered:
      print("Investigate")
  else:
      print("Camp accounted for")

What actually happens
Python evaluates the condition. If it is true, the indented block under if runs. Otherwise the indented block under else runs. Exactly one of those two branches runs. Comparisons such as <, >, >=, and == ask a yes-or-no question; they do not assign a new value. A single = assigns; == compares.

When this is useful
Use if/else when two outcomes are possible and the program must pick one before continuing.
concepts: if runs a block only when a condition is true
else runs when the condition is false
Exactly one of the two branches runs
>, <, >=, and == compare values; = assigns a name
Indented lines belong to the branch above them

examples.title: Abandoned camp
examples.explanation: Three bedrolls is fewer than four registered adventurers, so only Investigate is printed.

common_mistakes: Using = where you meant == — assignment is not a comparison
Forgetting the colon after if or else
Forgetting to indent the lines that belong inside the if or else

exercises.title: Predict the branch
hints: Check whether the condition returned > 0 is true or false.
When the condition is false, the else block runs.
returned is 0, so the program takes the else path.
exercises.failure_message: Trace from the condition. Only one branch runs.

exercises.title: Complete the condition
exercises.prompt: Print Investigate if bedrolls is fewer than registered; otherwise print Camp accounted for. Replace None with the correct comparison.
exercises.starter_code:
bedrolls = 3
registered = 4
if None:  # TODO: compare bedrolls with registered
    print("Investigate")
else:
    print("Camp accounted for")
hints: The condition should ask whether bedrolls is less than registered.
The if line should compare bedrolls to registered, then keep the two print blocks.

tests.message: Use if and else to choose what to print.

exercises.title: Debug the decision
exercises.prompt: This program should print Active search when status is OVERDUE. It currently fails because the comparison is written incorrectly. Repair the decision so the comparison uses ==.
hints: Look at the symbol between status and "OVERDUE".
A single = assigns; a comparison that asks "are these equal?" needs ==.
Change the if line to use status == "OVERDUE".

tests.message: Keep an if/else decision in the program.

exercises.failure_message: The decision cannot run correctly until the comparison is valid Python. Remember that = assigns and == compares.

exercises.title: Encounter: The Abandoned Camp
exercises.prompt:
Given expedition = 17, registered = 4, and bedrolls = 3, write a short encounter check.

If bedrolls is fewer than registered, print exactly:
Expedition 17: INVESTIGATE

Otherwise print exactly:
Expedition 17: CLEAR

Requirements:
- keep (or create) the three variables
- use if/else
- build the printed line with an f-string that inserts expedition
- do not hardcode 17 inside the printed sentence
exercises.starter_code:
expedition = 17
registered = 4
bedrolls = 3
# Decide INVESTIGATE or CLEAR
hints: Compare bedrolls with registered, then choose one printed line.
An f-string can start with Expedition and insert the expedition variable before the colon.
Use if bedrolls < registered to print INVESTIGATE, else print CLEAR — both via an f-string that includes expedition.

tests.message: Use if and else to choose INVESTIGATE or CLEAR.
Build the printed line with an f-string that includes expedition — do not hardcode 17 in the sentence.

exercises.success_message: Encounter logged. Four registered, three bedrolls — your program chose INVESTIGATE from the data.
